transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well... I suppose I'm here because there's just a pattern I've been seeing for months now. 

With my sister. Her appointments keep getting moved, the bills show up wrong... people supposedly just 'forget' to call me back. Everyone keeps telling me it's just administrative mistakes. But... I know it isn't. I know they're keeping information from me. They're trying to push me out of the decisions.
Aside from this situation with your sister, have you generally found yourself distrustful or suspicious of other people—friends, coworkers, or others—throughout your life, even before this started?
No... I don't think so. I manage an office, so I work with people every day just fine. It's really just... what's happening right now. With my sister's care.

Can you tell me what was happening in your life right around the time these suspicions about your sister first started—was there a specific event, like a change in her health or care arrangements, that triggered it?
Well... it's been going on for about 11 months now. Her health just... suddenly got worse. So I had to step in and start coordinating all her care. That's when all this started.

latest_inference.note: The presentation shows a fixed, circumscribed delusion (belief that others are conspiring to exclude her from her sister's care) lasting nearly a year, with no other psychotic symptoms and preserved occupational functioning. This pattern is inconsistent with an adjustment disorder (F43.2), which would not typically produce a specific, sustained delusional belief system; thus F43.2 is ruled out in favor of a primary delusional disorder.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a single, well-organized, non-bizarre persecutory delusion (belief that family members are deliberately concealing information and excluding her from her sister's care) that has persisted for approximately 11 months, exceeding the 1-month duration required for delusional disorder. There is no evidence of hallucinations, disorganized speech, negative symptoms, or broader psychotic disintegration seen in schizophrenia. Her overall functioning is preserved—she successfully manages an office and functions normally in other domains—and there is no pervasive lifelong pattern of distrust/suspiciousness predating this episode that would suggest paranoid personality disorder. The delusion is circumscribed to the specific situation involving her sister's care, consistent with a persecutory-type delusional disorder.
